thread.document:
Dear class,

By now, most of you have submitted your project proposals. (If you haven't set your group to include everyone, please do so. We notice some submissions didn't set the group correctly)

Be sure to bring a printed copy of your proposal with you to your scheduled meeting with a member of course staff this week. (And if you haven't signed up yet, please do sign up.)

If you're meeting virtually, please have a copy ready to share so that the staff member can quickly skim it to identify risk factors, etc.

The most important thing is to get started now. Start writing code, getting tests in place, etc... Deep Learning is full of frustration as you find bugs after having trained something for a day or two. It will take lots of iteration to get things done and ready by the deadlines. You need to start now. (Unlike other areas, pulling all-nighters at the end isn't sufficient because of the training time that is required.)

In terms of the meetings with course staff, our primary objective is to make sure that your project is safe vis-a-vis your learning and being able to get full credit on your project. This means:

Making sure that you can train something (could be from scratch, a finetune, or experimental probes of some sort) in a way that lets you demonstrate a working understanding of many of the core practical concepts in deep learning:

Including an exploration of hyperparameters --- at least learning rate, but more as relevant to what you are doing.

Making plots of training progress 

Having some way for you to justify your hyperparameter and optimizer choices --- it is perfectly find for some of these to be X paper did it and we are following... But you have to be able to do this.

Making sure that you have some kind of held-out data or other ways of evaluating whether whatever you have trained actually makes sense and/or you have trained it sufficiently.

Some thought about the architecture you are using including exploration/experimentation as relevant (this will be modulated on what you have to work with --- obviously, we cannot deem a project to be good if all you do is take code that already exists out there and just run it on some other data. In cases where solid code exists to build on, we will expect architectural experimentations.)

At least one hypothesis that you can express clearly and design an experiment to test. It is fine if the hypothesis fails or that the tests are inconclusive, but you have to be able to try enough to verify that this is not due to a bug on your part or grossly inadequate data or compute. Negative results or boring results are perfectly fine for full credit. Research has risks and many things fail --- that's ok. 

A path to a solid review of the literature that situates your work within the field and the current state of understanding and/or mystery.

If you have concerns in any of these directions, be sure to bring it up in your meeting so that we can help you mitigate those risks as early as possible.
